utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please be seated, Mr. Prcac. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. I would like to be sure that the interpreters are here. They haven't given up yet. That's good. Okay. The technical booth is working properly. The interpreters are here, the stenotypists are here, the court reporters had here. Madam Registrar, would you please announce the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is case number IT-95-4-PT, the Prosecutor versus Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I would now like to ask Ms. Hollis to tell us the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Brenda Hollis, Michael Keegan, Kapila Waidyaratne appear on behalf of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. And for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: Jovan Simic, attorney at law, appearing for Dragoljub Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Simic. We are meeting today for a Status Conference whose purpose is to ascertain the status of the case's preparation, in this case, the Prcac case, and to know whether the case is ready. If it is, we can think about joining this to the Kvocka case. We are really now at the Pre-trial Conference, that is, the point when we realise whether we are ready or not. In order to reach our objective, what I suggest for the agenda is the following: First of all, we've tried to organise the questions well, and if we have not, it will be shown by the results. But for the time being, I think we've got to deal with the obligations of disclosure on the part of the Prosecutor; then the preliminary motions, which will include a set of smaller questions having to do with the Prosecution case file, most all of those questions covered by the small paragraphs of -- or subparagraphs of 65 ter; and then we'll have a third point, which is the Defence file, that is, Rule 65 ter (F). We will consider joining the trials. And our fifth point would be other matters, other matters that the parties might find appropriate or important to raise and which have not been included among the other points on the agenda. To begin with, we can start with our agenda item 1, which is disclosure obligations on the part of the Prosecutor. That is, the Prosecutor had indicated at the last Status Conference, which was on the 22nd of March, that she would have to look into the situation of two potential witnesses, two or three. Where do we stand now with those witnesses, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have confirmed the attendance of witnesses for the trial. To the extent that witnesses have indicated they are available to testify, we have provided disclosure of those witnesses to the Defence. We would note for Your Honours that because of changed circumstances for some witnesses who had been identified earlier on, we will be filing with the Court a changed witness order for Mr. Prcac, as well as for the other accused. That does not include very many new witnesses, but it does include some new witnesses. They will be called in such a manner that disclosure will not delay the trial. But it is because of changed circumstances with witnesses that we had previously identified, as well as taking into account a few new witnesses relevant to Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Hollis. As regards this question, I think there are no problems. The parties, with the Judges, simply have to know what changes have been made, and I see no problem there. Another question that I had for you, Ms. Hollis, on that point, is the following: I'd like to know whether the Prosecutor, if that is the case, has transmitted to the Defence, whether any measures have been taken for that to be done, the exculpatory evidence, which is Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As we prepare our cases for trial, we of course look for evidence that's required to be disclosed pursuant to Rule 68, as we discover that potentially exculpatory evidence that is disclosed to the Defence. To date the Prosecution has disclosed all evidence that, to our knowledge, would fall within Rule 68. We understand also, Your Honours, that this is a continuing obligation, so as we were to discover additional evidence that would fall within that rule, of course we will continue to disclose it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. You may be seated for the time being. I will now ask Mr. Simic for the Defence whether he would like to react to what has just been said, or whether he has anything appropriate to say to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may also be seated. Thank you very much. We can now move to agenda number 2, that is, preliminary motions. Let me remind the parties that during the last Status Conference, the Defence waived the 30-day time period for filing preliminary motions. The Defence, however, has requested that clarifications be brought in respect of several contradictions that it found in the indictment. I would like to ask the parties where things stand with that question. Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to the extent you are referring to the pre-trial brief that was filed by the Defence, our position on that is that the contradictions are in the way the Prosecution and the Defence will evaluate the evidence. So there is no way other than the way we present the evidence and the way we argue its interpretation to resolve these differences. But that is the basis that I am referring to when I talk about these contradictions is that they have been put forth in their pre-trial brief, and I see these basically as evidentiary matters that can only be resolved through the trial itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was asking the question because the Defence noted contradictions in the indictment itself which could be the subject of a preliminary motion. And at that time, we said, "All right, the parties will consult with one another in order to clarify that issue." Is that what you are talking about? That is my question, Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: We have consulted with Defence counsel yesterday. Those contradictions were not raised during that discussion and the Defence counsel, we believe, indicated that he would not be filing preliminary motions, that he believed that issues would be resolved through the trial. So we have not dealt formally with contradictions because of the discussions we had yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me turn to Mr. Simic. What is your reaction, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with what Ms. Hollis said. We discussed these matters yesterday, particularly those that we were especially interested in so that we would deal with the problems that were there. We have had cooperation in this respect. We came to certain conclusions and as for all other matters that still remain contentious, I agree with Ms. Hollis we shall work this out during the trial and I believe that there is no need to prolong the pre-trial period any longer, so let us deal with what we have at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may be seated, Mr. Simic. I will now move to the third point on the agenda. We're moving along very well. The Prosecution's file, that is Rule 65 ter paragraph (E), what we called the Prosecution's pre-trial period. The Prosecutor was requested to provide during the Status Conference we held last time. I'm just going to make a checklist to make sure that we really are prepared. Let me note that in accordance with the provisions of Rule 65 ter (E), the Prosecutor must file first a pre-trial brief addressing the facts on the legal issues including a written statement setting out the nature of his or her case, and I think that we have that brief and we received it on the 24th of March. Perhaps I could move through the list, and if you have anything to say, you can ask for the floor. If there's nothing to be said, I'll just move on. Do you agree with working that way? I see that you are nodding in agreement. All right. Second, the admissions by the parties, and a statement of matters which are not in dispute. I believe that the Defence on the 6th of April filed a response to the Prosecutor's brief dealing with the issue of judicial notice. The Defence does not contest the ten paragraphs of the Prosecutor's annex dated 11 January 1999 so, therefore, I believe that the parties have agreed on several matters of law which are not in dispute. Is that correct, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: If I could make a slight correction to that, Your Honour. Your Honours will recall that during the 24 February conference, the parties were requested to, during an adjournment, to discuss further the adjudicated facts and which ones they could agree to. And that after we came back in in the afternoon session, Mr. Niemann, on behalf of the Prosecution, indicated the facts that all the parties had agreed to. After that session, the Prosecution basically took the 11 January adjudicated facts document, removed from it the facts which were not agreed upon, and then we served that modified document on Mr. Prcac's Defence counsel at his initial appearance. I believe there was some confusion because we had these two documents but, indeed, the agreed facts that we have provided to the Defence are the facts that all four Defence counsel for the other accused had agreed to. The facts that Mr. Prcac's attorney is disputing in his response are facts that were contained in the 11 January filing but facts which are not contained in the modified filing. I believe, Your Honours, you will find that there will be no facts in this modified document that will be in dispute according to my discussions with Mr. Simic. So we're not dealing anymore with all of the facts in the 11 January document, we're dealing with the modified version from which the Prosecution has removed all of the contested facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Ms. Hollis. Mr. Simic, in respect of that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what Ms. Hollis said is correct. I have just received this document. I glanced at it. However, in the pre-trial brief, I dealt with certain matters that I will be contesting during the trial; however, it is not in this document. However, everything that we agreed upon as adjudicated facts is not mentioned in here. That is to say, that this document is fully along the lines of what we agreed upon. That is what I wish to say on behalf of Defence and on behalf of Mr. Prcac. We agree with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Mr. Simic, thank you very much. And thank you very much, Ms. Hollis, for your clarifications. In respect of this question, I would like to go back to a discussion with you about paragraph (H) of Rule 65 ter. And in order to definitively settle the question, you see in paragraph (H) it says that, "The pre-trial judge shall record the points of agreement and disagreement on matters of law and fact. In this connection, he or she may order the parties to file written submissions with either the Pre-trial Judge or the Trial Chamber." What I suggest to you in light of this subparagraph would be to present a document to the Trial Chamber, when it's here, to present it with your written conclusions. And the time period would be until the beginning of May, when we resume the trial on the 2nd of May. Do you agree with that suggestion, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Do you agree, Mr. Simic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you know the Chamber could issue an order but, as I told you, this Chamber exercises its authority in an explanatory way and not in an authoritarian manner, and that's why I've asked for your opinion. We can now move to the third point -- no, to the fourth point, that is the list of witnesses. The names and pseudonyms of the witnesses. We have on the 24th of March received a list of 71 witnesses of fact with the indication of the pseudonyms if that is required. The list also has the name of six expert witnesses, Wright, Clark, Brown, Alonso, Smith and Malik, and eight deposition witnesses. At this point, I would like to ask two questions: Where do we stand in respect of the depositions through a presiding officer? That is, are we going to organise our work the same way as we already did in the Kvocka case; that is Mr. Fourmy would go with the parties to organise that entire part of the depositions taken by the presiding officer; that is including the eight witnesses that we just mentioned. That's the first question. The second question relates to the expert witnesses. In light of Rule 94 bis, what is the Defence position? Perhaps I can ask the parties the question, both parties. First, I'll ask it of Ms. Hollis, that is the questions having to do with depositions through the presiding officer, the expert witnesses in respect of Rule 94 bis. Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. In regard to deposition witnesses, the Prosecution's response will vary somewhat depending on the timing of those depositions. We would suggest, perhaps, that the most efficient way to operate would be to schedule the taking of Prosecution depositions for the end of our case. In that manner, if we believe that the evidence adduced to date was sufficient, we could then eliminate some of those depositions. We would suggest the same procedure for expert evidence. If we believe that on the record at the -- toward the end of our case we have no need for some of those expert witnesses, we could then not call them. So we would suggest -- we certainly agree with the procedure for depositions that have been set up and we would suggest the best timing for our depositions would be toward the end of our case because it could result in actually deleting some of those witnesses from our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say to you, Ms. Hollis, that your proposal is fabulous. I think it's really wonderful in respect to organising our work and in respect of the expert witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What we suggest is that as we near the point where we make our decision, we would provide the reports or the statements of the experts to the Defence but only of those experts we have decided to call. So we would not provide the statements now, we would wait until closer in time to when we would call them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Ms. Hollis, thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Simic, you are involved in depositions as well because these depositions taken through the presiding officer are always used with both parties present; therefore, the Defence must be there and especially in respect of Ms. Hollis's proposal. Excuse me, I expressed my positive point of view and I hope that I have not influenced you. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, the Defence agrees that this would be the most expedient way to proceed. In this way, perhaps some witnesses will prove to be unnecessary as we see how the trial evolves. Also, we agreed yesterday with the Office of the Prosecutor that we would act in the same way, that we would try to focus only on the most important facts. Whatever other evidence proves to be unnecessary, we shall simply delete it as well as those witnesses; anything that is not absolutely necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Simic. In respect to the expert witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Rule 94 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the statements of expert witnesses are handed over to us -- I haven't seen them yet in all fairness -- we will be able to state our views, and indeed we are going to act in accordance with 94 ter. We think that the most expedient way to proceed would be as proposed by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may be seated, Mr. Simic. I would now like to move to another aspect, that is, the summary of the witness statements. On the 24th of March, we also received those summaries and so that's good. Subject to any additional witnesses that the Prosecution might call, and the Prosecutor is aware of the permanent obligation to disclose information, so I have nothing further to say about that. The other aspect has to do with those points of the indictment about which each witness will be heard, and specifically the references to the counts and to the paragraphs in the indictment. This was also done and so we are ready on that point as well. I now move to the estimated time of each testimony. Subject to the witnesses already mentioned, the Prosecutor intends to have testify 71 witnesses for various amounts of time between an hour and a half to two and a half hours. Therefore, we've got to count on a minimum of 128 hours, that is 32 days of hearing for the examination-in-chief of those witnesses at a rate of four hours of actual work each day. We work five hours but we do take breaks during those five hours. The Prosecutor is therefore asking for a minimum of seven weeks for the presentation of her case without counting the time for depositions under Rule 71. I think that that means, on the whole, that addition of witnesses to that case would mean an additional week in relation to what we had provided for already. I don't know whether you agree with that assessment, or whether the Prosecutor has any other opinion on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we do agree with that assessment. We would like again to put on the record, of course, that those are estimates that we are giving, because in reality, until they testify, you don't really know how much time it may take. We would also point out that we have looked very carefully at the indictment, the allegations we have made, and we are trying to proceed with the fewest number of witnesses to prove those allegations. However, as events unfurl at trial, we may find it necessary to perhaps bring someone from the additional witness list, or perhaps to delete even members of the yes list. But again those are estimates, our best estimates of the time that would be involved, and we agree with your assessment of that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree completely with you, Ms. Hollis. We're trying to organise our work, and of course that always means that we are not slaves to that organisation. The organisation has been established to serve us, and if there are any special circumstances, we can make changes and adapt it as required. Thank you very much for your comment. Mr. Simic, do you have anything you'd like to say about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday we talked to the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor and we also discussed this particular subject: How long the Prosecution witnesses will testify. I believe that seven weeks will not be long enough, if we take into account the fact that the Defence is going to cross-examine the witnesses, and there are five Defence attorneys. There are also some witnesses that the Prosecutor said will not testify for very long, but there are four or five witnesses that have to deal directly with my client, Mr. Prcac, judging by what I've seen so far, so perhaps it's going to take longer altogether. As you said, these organisational matters are very important, but I think that perhaps an extra week will be needed for the Prosecution case, or perhaps even yet another week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Simic. We're taking note of your concerns. As I said, we are always available for any changes that need to be made, but I think that it's always important to have a limit and an objective for our work. We're working here with that spirit in our minds, that when we begin pre-trial management, one must state what is the date that it has to be completed. And when we begin a trial, we say more or less what the date of its end will be. But this is always approximate. Still, if we have that limit, perhaps we can force ourselves a little bit more. If we have no limit at all, we all know what human nature is like; it always takes advantage of things to do nothing. But that's not the case with you, of course I understand that, because your nature is special. But we do have to take some organisational measures, and this is why I'm always open to say: No, for this reason we've got to go back to look at our calendar. But I would like to maintain a date once it's been set, at least for the time being. Let me move now to the last point under 65 ter (E), that is, the list of exhibits which the Prosecutor intends to offer, stating, where possible, whether the Defence has any objection as to the authenticity. This was filed on the 24th of March. What I would like to recommend -- this is a practice which you've already used, as you know -- to have prepared in advance coordination with the court registrar the numbering of the exhibits, and I think we've already been doing that, and we've got to keep that in mind. Let me now move to the third point on the agenda, that is, the Defence file. Let me note that on the 6th of April, the Defence filed its Pre-Trial brief dealing with the points of fact and law, and containing a written presentation which specifically indicates the nature of that defence of the accused, as well as an indication of the reason for any possible points of dispute. I believe that I have nothing further to add to that, but since Mr. Simic is interested in this, I'll give him the floor to ask whether he has anything he'd like to say or add.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do our best within the scope of our possibilities to honour all our obligations in accordance with the Rules and the Statute. We sent a Pre-Trial brief, therefore, and we are going to present our evidence. At this point in time, I believe that we have done enough in order to move on to the trial stage, so that we could work on an equal footing, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You've worked sufficiently and enough, and you didn't need to say anything further, since you are a modest person. As far as the Prosecution are concerned, are there any comments that need to be made?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. We have no comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. We will now move to the fourth point on the agenda. The interpreters were afraid that we would repeat what happened yesterday, that it took so long. That is, I'm talking about joinder of trials. In respect of the Prosecution's file and the Defence file, the question of the impact of a joinder of trial on the case, that is, joining Prcac to Kvocka, I think this is something we've already looked at. That is, the Prosecutor's file in the Prcac file says that these two cases have common things together, except for about ten witnesses, and so we have already understood that this would extend the Kvocka hearings by one week, approximately, if the two cases were to be joined. And when I say that this is if the two cases were joined, I could perhaps inform the parties that subject to the disclosure obligations by the Prosecutor having been satisfied, that is, disclosure on a constant basis, which is necessary if it should prove necessary, we consider that this case is ready to go to trial. For that question, rather, this assertion that the case is trial ready, do the parties have any comments they'd like to make? What is your opinion? Is it or is it not, from your point of view, Ms. Hollis?

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, from our point of view, we believe that the case is trial ready. We would suggest, however, in an abundance of caution, that as a matter of prudence, because of the circumstances of this particular question of joinder, that the Trial Chamber also satisfy itself that the accused himself is comfortable with this concept. And by suggesting that, we in no way mean to imply anything negative about Defence counsel's professionalism, integrity or competence. We believe he certainly is competent, has full integrity, but because of these particular circumstances, perhaps it would benefit the Chamber to inquire of Mr. Prcac. Having said that, Your Honours, of course the Prosecution position is that even if Mr. Prcac and his counsel oppose joinder, joinder would still be appropriate in this case, and of course we would ask for joinder even if there was an objection to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Ms. Hollis. I think the proposal to hear Mr. Prcac is an excellent one. I hesitate to hear Mr. Prcac before having heard Mr. Simic. Since Ms. Hollis said that she's not calling into question your ethics or competence, still I believe if I were in your place, I would like to first hear what Mr. Prcac has to say. I don't know what your opinion on that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the best thing would be to address my client first. We have already agreed on our position, but the best thing would be for him to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Prcac, would you rise, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Have you understood this entire discussion, in particular -- do you hear me? -- specifically in respect of joining your case to the other case, that you are aware of? What is your feeling? Would you tell us what it is and would you speak freely, please, in your own words.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have been following this discussion, and right now, at this very moment, I'm speaking about this position of joining my case to the Kvocka case. I am of the opinion that perhaps it would be good for it to be together, perhaps; but, on the other hand, perhaps it could even be to my detriment, in part. But at any rate, I would have to think about this some more, and perhaps next time when we have this kind of a Status Conference, I could give you my definite position. Right now my position is not clearly defined. I understand what could be achieved through this joinder, but I just want to figure it out for myself what would be good for me and what would be detrimental. That would be all. Thank you. I mean, I do apologise. There's one more thing I wish to say. I don't know much about the Kvocka case, you see, so that makes things a bit more difficult for me. I don't know very much about the Kvocka case. I haven't really acquainted myself with these materials, so please allow me to familiarise myself with the subject matter, and then I will present my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prcac, we're speaking about a joinder of trials when the facts are the same and when they occurred within the same time period. What we are dealing with here is Omarska and the dates, which are the same; that is, the locations and the time are the same in the Kvocka case and in your case. And as you know, you were not in the other case, only because at the time -- only for the reason that the arrests took place at different times, but the case was always the same from the very beginning. It was only because there were arrests at different times were they different cases, but the facts are the same. Ultimately it's one case with five people, and those five people are put into the same place and the same time. And something else that I would like to tell you, Mr. Prcac, is that this is the last Status Conference scheduled; therefore, we're not going to have another Status Conference. I don't know whether this information changes your position or not, but in any case, I would like to continue to hear what you have to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I followed everything you had to say very carefully and I understood you. Well, let them be joined. You explained this to me nicely in your introduction, so I understood it a bit better now, that this is a case that is quite similar to this one. And as you said, I'm in a fairly similar situation as the persons involved in that case, so I really have no objection. Let them be joined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can also tell you, Mr. Prcac, that you will keep your individual position in the case. Each accused keeps his own individual position in the case. It's the same case, but each person has his own individual place in it, and yours will not be mixed in with the others.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for having acquainted me with all of this, because I was really thinking about that too. Yes, the case is the same, but then perhaps someone did more bad things and someone did less, or whatever. That's what I was thinking about too. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, as a conclusion, Mr. Prcac, which I can say to you so that things are very clear for you and so that you can take a decision in full awareness of what you are deciding, you are not going to take responsibility for other people, nor will other people take responsibility for you. Each person will have his own responsibility. Therefore, what is your position? Do you agree or do you not agree to having the trials joined?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with having the trials joined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already explained to you on another occasion that you have advantages. You are in a really exceptional situation because you've just arrived and your trial is beginning. Otherwise you would have to wait quite a long time for your trial to open. We are taking note of your decision, and you agree to the trials being joined; is that what I'm to understand, Mr. Prcac?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You may be seated, Mr. Prcac.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Simic, now the technician gets the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at our previous Status Conference I said that it would be in the imperative interest of my client to have the trials joined. Now I'm even more certain of this. So I would indeed wish to have a joinder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. You may be seated. I believe that the Chamber can make its decision now. The trials will be joined. This will be done orally, but a written decision will follow. We consider this to be an important decision, and so from the point of view of organising our work, the decision is already taken, but we want to issue it in writing as well. The Chamber -- before making that decision, I would like to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Trial Chamber renders the following decision: Considering that the accused has the right to be tried without any unjustified delay, in accordance with the provisions of Rule 21, paragraph (4)(C) of the Statute, that the accused, Dragoljub Prcac, Miroslav Kvocka, Milojica Kos, Mlado Radic, and Zoran Zigic are accused of crimes committed as part of a single transaction at the Omarska camp, specifically, between the 31st of May 1992 and the 31st of December 1992; that the Prosecution's file dealing with the accused, Prcac, is almost the same as the accused in the Kvocka case: Kos, Radic, Zigic; that the trial of Kvocka, Kos, Radic, and Zigic began on the 28th of February, 2000 by the testimony of the accused Kvocka, Kos, Radic, and Zigic. I will repeat that point. The trial of the accused Kvocka, Kos, Radic, and Zigic began on the 28th of February, 2000 by the testimony of the accused Kvocka and Radic and was interrupted after that testimony, but since the oral evidence was filed into the Prosecution's case as exhibits; that the Defence of Mr. Prcac, specifically Mr. Prcac, do not object to the trials being joined, requested by the Prosecutor on the 6th of March 2000; that a joinder of trials would allow avoiding duplicating evidence, would minimize a repetition of evidence given by the same witnesses and, in general, would assist saving judicial time. It is, therefore, in the interests of the accused to be tried expeditiously, and in the interest of justice to join the accused Prcac's trial to the trial of the accused Kvocka, Kos, Radic, and Zigic. The Chamber will also render a written decision. And there you have it. This is the Trial Chamber's decision. We can now move to the fifth point on the agenda, that is, other matters. That is, do the parties have any additional questions that have not been dealt with under the points on the agenda and which they consider important to be dealt with? Ms. Hollis.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter only, and that is the Prosecution had understood that perhaps there would be another conference of all the counsel and accused prior to the commencement of evidence on the 2nd of May. My understanding now is that there will not be another conference before the 2nd of May. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I had suggested at that time the 12th and 14th for a Status Conference, and on the suggestion of Mr. Simic, we had agreed that the 12th would be enough. Another point is that the Status Conference which we are now organising in Kvocka now includes Prcac.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: So that is my question: Will there be a Status Conference now including all five accused and their attorneys?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The date has not yet been set, but it will be in the beginning of May after having resumed the hearings.

utterances.speaker: MS. HOLLIS
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. There will be matters that the Prosecution will raise at that time concerning suggestions on to how most expeditiously move through the proceedings. We will file a written notice of those suggestions prior to that Status Conference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. That is very useful to know in advance, what your questions are, so that we can be -- they can be dealt with in pre-trial conferences. Now, let me give the floor to Mr. Simic. Do you have any other issues you'd like to raise and would you be available for filing a document with suggestions of the same type as Ms. Hollis'?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no questions, Your Honour. As for the written document, since we are a team and we are all working together on the ground, we shall do our best. I will be coming to The Hague again on the 26th, because we agreed with the Prosecutor that the accused should make a statement of his own, and by then I will have prepared all the necessary questions and shall submit them in writing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Simic. Thank you, Ms. Hollis. I, myself, have a question which I forgot to deal with which touches on the Defence position. I would like to ask Mr. Simic whether he has any position in respect of the testimony of Mr. Prcac, specifically, whether he would like to use the same way of working as Mr. Kvocka and Mr. Radic did. That is, whether, first of all, if he -- the first question is does he want to testify, and, if so, if he does, does he want to testify at the beginning of the trial, as the others did, because we still have that possibility, or at another time?

utterances.speaker: MR. SIMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at the last Status Conference I also said that I was very sorry that at that point in time Mr. Prcac could not testify. As I said, we agreed with the Prosecutor that we give a statement on the 27th, the 28th, perhaps also the 29th of April. We'll see how fast it goes. That would mean that if the trial were to begin on the 2nd of May, as we expect and as has been scheduled, I think that it would be very strenuous for my client to make two very serious statements within five days. Mr. Prcac wishes to make a statement. The Defence wishes that too and that will certainly happen. Perhaps we could make a statement after the Prosecution case and then we shall start with the cross-examination of all the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. It was my fault. I hadn't remembered that information. I apologise for having asked you the question again. You may be seated. Let me now turn to Mr. Prcac and ask you, Mr. Prcac, about your detention conditions and how your health is.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, allow me to address you. The last Status Conference was held on the 22nd of March this year and you put this same question to me. I did not really answer it. I forgot to tell you the truth, that I was really in a different context, in a different frame of mind. I am quite willing to tell you about how I have felt in the detention unit ever since I arrived. I can say that, indeed, I did not expect the kind of conditions that I do have, and I'm speaking about the staff there, the food, the medical service. I'm still receiving medicines. I'm still being treated. I also make telephone calls to my family. I could not have imagined all of that. I wish to extend my thanks for that, and I've had no objections whatsoever. Had I had any objections, I certainly would have told you about it, but this has not been the case, and I wish it were that way for everyone else too. I thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may be seated, Mr. Prcac, and you can always communicate with us through your attorney if there are any problems. You can always inform us of any questions you have.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I think we have finished our Status Conference. It took us an hour. The interpreters can be released now. We've done a lot of work this week and we're going to continue to work. We still have two days left in the week, but I would thank the parties for their cooperation, for the work that you have done, and I thank everybody. I, myself, will continue working, and I wish you a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: adjourned at 5.02 p.m.
